passage:
Monday. Jahnavi and Rafiq both showed Ma their drawings. Ma used to say whose was better. This time she said, "Jahnavi, you worked so long on the shading. Rafiq, look how brave those colours are." Both grinned.
Wednesday. They argued over the swing. Ma stayed at the window, watching, and did not step in. After some shouting, Rafiq said, "Five pushes each?" Jahnavi agreed.
Saturday. Rafiq climbed too high on the wall. Ma came out at once and helped him down. Later, when Jahnavi's kite tangled, Rafiq helped her fix it without anyone asking. Ma noticed they hadn't said "I'm better" all week.

qa.q: What deal did Rafiq suggest for the swing?
qa.a: He suggested five pushes each.

qa.q: What does Rafiq helping with the kite unasked suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt at ease rather than in competition with Jahnavi, so he was willing to help her now that he isn't being compared.

qa.q: What did Ma do differently that helped?
qa.a: She praised each child's own effort, let them solve the swing quarrel themselves and stepped in only when Rafiq was unsafe on the wall.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi experience her mother's new way of praising?
qa.a: Jahnavi likely feels seen for their own work, like the shading, so there is no need to beat Rafiq to feel good.

grounding: It shows a parent praising each child's own effort, letting them settle small quarrels and stepping in only for safety, easing rivalry.

passage: Vaibhav, you asked your Indu Dadi why I never say which of you cousins is the cleverest. Sit, I'll tell you. When your Papa and his brother were small, I always compared. "Look at Suresh's marks, why can't you?" They fought all the time, over everything. One day a teacher told me, "Praise each one for what he does." So I tried. I told your Papa his handwriting was careful, and Suresh that he was a good runner. When they quarrelled over small things, I let them sort it out, and only stepped in if someone might get hurt. Slowly, they stopped trying to beat each other. Now they talk every day.

qa.q: What did Indu Dadi praise Vaibhav's Papa for?
qa.a: She praised his careful handwriting.

qa.q: How did Indu Dadi feel about her old habit of comparing?
qa.a: She seems to regret it, since it made her sons fight over everything, which is why she changed.

qa.q: What approach did Indu Dadi switch to, and why did it work?
qa.a: She praised each son for his own strengths and let them solve small quarrels, so they no longer had to compete for her approval.

qa.q: How might Suresh have felt when his mother stopped comparing?
qa.a: He probably felt less pressure and more valued for his running, and less need to beat his brother.

grounding: It illustrates a parent who stops comparing, praises each child's own strengths and lets small quarrels be settled by them, so the siblings stop competing.

passage:
The power had gone during exam week, and both boys were studying by candlelight at the dining table, Darshan for Class 7 maths, Zubin for Class 4 English.

Their mother used to say, "Look at Darshan, he never needs help." Not anymore. She had stopped comparing them after Zubin cried himself to sleep one night.

Now she looked at each of their notebooks separately. "Darshan, you worked out that long sum on your own. That took patience." Then, "Zubin, you rewrote that answer three times until it was neat. I noticed."

Later the boys argued over the last candle. Mummy stayed in the kitchen. They sorted it out: one candle, both sides of the table.

Neither of them needed to be better than the other that night.

qa.q: How did the boys study during the power cut?
qa.a: By candlelight at the dining table.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when his mother praised his neat answer?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and noticed for his own effort, without being compared to Darshan.

qa.q: Why was staying in the kitchen during the candle argument a good choice?
qa.a: It let the boys solve a small quarrel themselves, since it wasn't a safety issue, and they found a fair answer.

qa.q: How might Darshan see his mother's new way of praising?
qa.a: He may feel valued for his own patience, and less pressure to always be the one who never needs help.

grounding: During a power cut, the mother praises each son's own effort instead of comparing them and lets them solve a small quarrel, so they have less need to beat each other.

passage:
For years Indu had said, "Why can't you be like your sister?" to Baljeet, and "Look how fast Baljeet runs" to Simran. The fights in their Amritsar home got worse every year.

So she changed. When Simran brought home a drawing, Indu said, "You used so many colours. You must have thought hard about that." When Baljeet came back from football, she said, "You kept trying even after the first goal went in."

When they argued over the TV remote, she stayed in the kitchen, only calling, "Sort it out yourselves, please."

After a month, she noticed something. They argued less. Yesterday, Baljeet even told Simran, "Your drawing's nice." Simran looked so surprised she dropped her crayons.

qa.q: What did Indu used to say to Baljeet?
qa.a: "Why can't you be like your sister?"

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Baljeet praised her drawing?
qa.a: She was so surprised she dropped her crayons, probably also pleased and happy.

qa.q: What changes did Indu make, and why did they help?
qa.a: She praised each child's own effort and let them settle small quarrels themselves, so they felt less need to compete.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel being praised for trying, not for winning?
qa.a: He probably feels valued for his effort and less pressure to beat his sister.

grounding: Indu stops comparing her children, praises each for their own effort and lets them solve small quarrels, and their need to beat each other eases.

passage:
"Papa, Vikas got a gold star and I only got silver!"

"Yash, what did you get the silver star for?"

"For my science model."

"Tell me about the model."

"It's a windmill. The blades really turn."

"That sounds like a lot of work. You figured out how to make them turn?"

"Yes! Three days!"

"That's proper engineering. Well done, beta."

"...But Vikas got gold."

"Vikas, what was your star for?"

"Reading the most books."

"You love reading. That's your thing. Yash, windmills are yours."

"Papa, Yash took my eraser!"

"Boys, can you two sort that out? I'll be in the kitchen."

"...Here's your eraser, Vikas."

"Thanks. Can I see your windmill?"

qa.q: What did Yash make for his science model?
qa.a: A windmill.

qa.q: How does Yash feel by the end of the conversation?
qa.a: He feels proud of his windmill and less jealous, so he returns the eraser and shares with Vikas.

qa.q: What does Papa do that reduces rivalry?
qa.a: He praises each boy's own effort and strength instead of comparing stars, and lets them solve the eraser quarrel themselves.

qa.q: How does Vikas respond once the eraser is returned?
qa.a: He thanks Yash and shows interest in the windmill, feeling friendly rather than competitive.

grounding: In dialogue Papa praises each son for his own effort instead of comparing stars and lets them sort out a small quarrel, easing their need to beat each other.

passage: Abbu used to say, "Why can't you be neat like Rehan?" and Rehan got, "Why can't you read like Ayesha?" So we were always racing. This year something changed. After a parent-teacher meeting, Abbu stopped comparing. When I finished a whole chapter book, he said, "Ayesha, you stuck with that even when it got boring." When Rehan built the model bridge, he said, "You tried three designs. That's patience." Just about us, one at a time. And when we fought over the TV remote, he didn't come running. He said, "Sort it out, you two. Call me if someone's getting hurt." We made a timetable. My friend Sonali couldn't believe we have a remote timetable. Now I don't need to beat Rehan. I only need to beat my last book.

qa.q: What did Abbu say when Rehan built the model bridge?
qa.a: He said, "You tried three designs. That's patience."

qa.q: Why does Ayesha no longer feel a need to beat Rehan?
qa.a: Ayesha feels secure and valued for effort, so competing with Rehan no longer seems necessary.

qa.q: Which of Abbu's changes seems to have helped most?
qa.a: Praising each child's own effort without comparing, and letting them sort out small quarrels like the remote unless someone is getting hurt.

qa.q: How might Rehan feel now that he isn't compared with Ayesha?
qa.a: Rehan likely feels relieved and proud of his own patience, no longer measured against Ayesha's reading.

grounding: Shows a parent who stops comparing, praises each child's own effort and lets the children solve small quarrels, so the rivalry fades.
